data.text/markdown:
E5. How many numbers describe the flow? POD of the velocity field

Question

April's slides sized the flow latent at "between 64 and 256 dimensions". How many linear modes does the captured velocity field need, and does a basis built from some configs describe configs it has never seen?

Method

Proper orthogonal decomposition (the method of snapshots) of the velocity field, mean removed, on two regions: the near-wing patch at full resolution (x 1 to 7, y 0 to 4, z 2.5 to 5.5; 192 x 128 x 96 cells, 7.1 million values per snapshot) and the whole domain downsampled 4x (64 x 32 x 64). Each config's velocity is divided by its reference speed (the one the force coefficients use), so configs carry comparable weight.
  • Basis: the 430 second-beat snapshots of the 21 training configs.
  • Latent-sizing number: the relative reconstruction error (error norm over field norm, both about the training mean) of the 128 snapshots of the 6 held-out configs when projected on the first r modes of that basis.
  • Force probe: linear regression from the first r mode coefficients to the six force coefficients at the same instant, fitted on training configs, scored on held-out ones.
The patch is too large to decompose directly, so everything is computed from inner products between snapshots; a test pins that route to the direct one. Data used: 558 live plotfiles of Z:\...\prelim_sweep_fine\runs\, second beat of all 27 configs (18 to 24 per config), each checked for ns.cfl = 0.6, dt = 5e-4, the 256x128x256 grid and IAMReX f93dc794; all .old.* directories excluded; the final plotfile of the f* = 0.85 and 1.0 runs is excluded; for f* = 1.15 the final plotfile (step 3478, phase 0.9999, 78 steps after the previous one) is included. Force labels from examples/prelim_sweep_fine/dataset.parquet at 80d653a.

Result

A 64-to-256-dimensional linear latent reconstructs an unseen config's near-wing velocity to within 16% down to 9%.
modes r held-out error, patch training error, patch held-out error, whole domain force probe R2 (patch)
8 43% 45% 41% 0.86
16 31% 32% 30% 0.92
32 24% 21% 22% 0.94
64 16% 12% 15% 0.96
128 12% 6.1% 10% 0.983
256 8.7% 1.9% 6.6% 0.994
  • The basis transfers. Up to 16 modes, held-out configs are reconstructed as well as the training configs themselves. Beyond that a gap opens (at 256 modes, 8.7% held out against 1.9% in sample): the later modes are describing individual training snapshots.
  • There is no sharp low-rank cut-off. The pooled spectrum needs 17 modes for 90% of the fluctuation energy and 82 for 99%. Each halving of the error costs roughly a fourfold increase in modes.
  • One config alone is nearly full rank. A single config's second beat needs 14 modes for 99% of its energy out of only 20 snapshots, so the snapshot count, not the flow, is setting that number.
  • The near-wing patch is not harder than the whole domain (same errors within a few points), so the wake below the patch is not where the difficulty is.
  • Forces need far fewer modes than the field. Eight modes give a linear force probe R2 of 0.86 and 16 give 0.92.

data.text/html: Per-config spectra, near-wing patch (modes for 90% and 99% of each config's own fluctuation energy)

Follow-up: the same POD in a wing-fixed frame

The velocity was resampled onto a box that moves with the wing (2 chords x 3.2 span x 2 normal, velocity expressed in wing axes) and the decomposition repeated, on the patch block-averaged 4x. Moving with the wing roughly halves the number of modes needed.
lab frame (fixed patch) wing frame (moving box)
modes for 90% of fluctuation energy 15 7
modes for 99% 67 30
held-out error at 16 modes 29% 16%
held-out error at 64 modes 14% 5.8%
held-out error at 256 modes 6.2% 2.6%
So a good part of the slow decay in the lab frame is the wing sweeping through a fixed grid, as expected. The two columns are not the same region: the wing box is smaller and holds only the flow next to the wing, while the fixed patch also holds the wake the wing has left behind. Part of the gain is therefore the easier region, not only the frame.

data.text/markdown:
Caveats

  • These numbers are lower bounds on the latent a finer time sampling would need. There are only 18 to 24 snapshots per beat. A basis cannot have more modes than snapshots, and structures that live between snapshots are not represented at all.
  • The three frequency groups sample different phases (a plotfile every 100 steps is a different fraction of the beat at each frequency), so a held-out config is partly being asked to interpolate in phase as well as in parameters.
  • A wing moving through a fixed grid is the textbook slow-decay case for POD. A sharp structure that translates needs many fixed modes to describe. The slow decay here is evidence about this frame of reference, not proof that the flow is intrinsically high-dimensional; a wing-fixed frame or a nonlinear encoder could do much better with the same data. That is what E6 tests.
  • Errors are about the training mean; the mean field itself holds roughly half of the held-out energy, so errors relative to the total field would be smaller.
  • The cells inside the immersed boundary are included; nothing is masked.
  • The force probe uses 128 held-out snapshots and predicts forces a kinematics-only model already gets to within 1 to 2 percent (E1); it shows the field modes carry the force information, not that a field model is needed for it.
  • Velocity only; the pressure gradient was cached downsampled but not analysed.
  • Second beat only, from runs that are not yet periodic (E0).

Next step

Compare against a nonlinear encoder at the same latent size on the same patch (E6). The wing-frame result suggests any encoder should be given the wing pose, or work in wing coordinates, before it is asked to compress the field. For a future corpus, a plotfile interval of 25 to 50 steps would lift the snapshot-count cap that limits every number here.
